meta.title: Who really said "Three things cannot be long hidden: the sun, the moon, and the truth"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The Buddha taught it in substance (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.131), but the exact words are a 1907 paraphrase by P. Lakshmi Narasu — and it’s also wrongly pinned on Confucius.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Three things cannot be long hidden: the sun, the moon, and the truth'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Buddhist teaching, but not the Buddha’s exact words: the wording is P. Lakshmi Narasu’s 1907 paraphrase, later mis-credited to Confucius and Colin Powell.

answer.label: Paraphrase of the Buddha — not his exact words
answer.authorDates: fl. c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism — the teaching is genuinely his; the exact wording is a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The Buddha did teach a version of this — that three things shine openly, the moon, the sun, and the Dhamma of a Realized One (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.131 ↗) — but the familiar “cannot be long hidden … the truth” phrasing is a 20th-century paraphrase that quietly changes the meaning, first crystallising in P. Lakshmi Narasu’s The Essence of Buddhism (1907).

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.131, the Book of the Threes
P. Lakshmi Narasu, The Essence of Buddhism (1907)
first traced to A Way Forward (Voigt & Drury, 2003)

source.excerpt: Mendicants, these three things shine in the open, not under cover. What three? The moon shines in the open, not under cover. The sun shines in the open, not under cover. The teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One shine in the open, not under cover.
trail: The genuine teaching is Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.131 ↗: the moon, the sun, and “the teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One” shine in the open, not under cover — a point about the Dhamma being public, not about truth escaping concealment.
The compressed “three things … cannot be hidden … the truth” wording traces to P. Lakshmi Narasu’s The Essence of Buddhism (1907) ↗: “Three things shine before the world and cannot be hidden.”
In its exact modern form the line only surfaces around 2003 and drifts between the Buddha, Confucius and even Colin Powell, per Fake Buddha Quotes ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version keeps the sun and moon but swaps the Buddha’s Dhamma for a generic ‘truth’
source.excerptNote: The passage above (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.131) is what the Buddha is actually recorded as saying. Narasu compressed it in 1907 into “Three things shine before the world and cannot be hidden. They are the moon, the sun, and the truth proclaimed by the Tathāgata,” and later hands trimmed ‘the truth proclaimed by the Tathāgata’ down to just ‘the truth’ — turning a claim about open teaching into a claim about truth surfacing.

source.rightsNote: The underlying teaching is ancient and Narasu’s 1907 paraphrase is long out of copyright, so the words are free to use. Just don’t present them as the Buddha’s verbatim speech — they are a modern rewording, not a line from the Pāli Canon.

author.name: The Buddha (Siddhārtha Gautama)
author.kicker: The true source of the teaching
author.heading: About the Buddha
author.metaLine: fl. c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism
author.bio: The Buddha (Siddhārtha Gautama) was the north Indian teacher whose discourses, preserved in the Pāli Canon, include the ‘Book of the Threes’ passage this quote paraphrases. He taught that his Dhamma was open to all — “shining in the open, not under cover” — the opposite of a secret, initiate-only doctrine. The catchier ‘sun, moon and truth’ rewording is the later work of the Tamil Buddhist scholar P. Lakshmi Narasu, whose 1907 book compressed the discourse into a single memorable line.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This one is unusually tangled: the sentiment is genuinely the Buddha’s, but the exact words are not, and along the way the line has been pinned on two other famous names.

items.why: Quote sites such as AZ Quotes ↗ credit Confucius, but the line has no basis in the Analects or any Confucian text; it is a reworking of a Buddhist passage, not a Chinese one.
Fake Buddha Quotes ↗ notes the line has turned up credited to Colin Powell — a stray modern misattribution with no source behind it.
Crediting the Buddha is half-right: he taught the idea (AN 3.131 ↗), but these are not his words — the ‘sun, moon and truth’ phrasing is Narasu’s 1907 paraphrase.

misattribution.truthLine: The teaching is the Buddha’s (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.131 ↗); the memorable wording is P. Lakshmi Narasu’s 1907 paraphrase — not a line from Confucius, Colin Powell, or the Buddha’s own mouth.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The gap between the canonical text and the popular quote is not just wording — it is meaning. The Buddha’s original point was institutional: unlike the secret, initiate-only doctrines of some rival schools, his teaching was proclaimed openly, “in the open, not under cover.” The modern version repurposes that image into a moral promise that truth will always come to light, which is a different (and more marketable) claim.
That drift is exactly what makes the line so quotable today — and so easy to hang on whichever sage a reader finds most authoritative, whether the Buddha, Confucius, or a modern statesman.
context.pull: A claim about open teaching became a promise that truth always surfaces.
